revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Wrapping the Time Capsule
revealWordProblem.text: A time capsule box is shaped like a rectangular prism that is 9 in long, 4 in wide, and 5 in tall. You unfold it into a net so you can see all six faces laid flat. How many square inches of wrapping paper are needed to cover the whole box? Explain your reasoning.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Unfolding the box into a net shows 3 pairs of faces. SA = 2(9×4) + 2(9×5) + 2(4×5) = 72 + 90 + 40 = 202. You need 202 in² of wrapping paper.

launch.narrative: Missed a lesson — or just want a refresher? This catch-up station reviews Lessons 10.1–10.3: 10.1 Volume with Whole Number Edges, 10.2 Volume of Rectangular Prisms, 10.3 Surface Area Using Nets. Read the Big Ideas, warm up with the review problem, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 10.1–10.3
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 10.1: To find the volume of a box, multiply all three edges: V = length × width × height. • 10.2: A fractional edge does not change the rule: still multiply length × width × height. • 10.3: A box has 3 pairs of matching faces, so add up all 6 faces to get the surface area.

iDo.title: The Big Ideas (one per lesson)
lines: Lesson 10.1 — Volume with Whole Number Edges: To find the volume of a box, multiply all three edges: V = length × width × height.
Lesson 10.2 — Volume of Rectangular Prisms: A fractional edge does not change the rule: still multiply length × width × height.
Lesson 10.3 — Surface Area Using Nets: A box has 3 pairs of matching faces, so add up all 6 faces to get the surface area.

youDo.title: Show you're caught up
lines: The practice below mixes problems from Lessons 10.1–10.3. Each problem is tagged with its lesson number.
Stuck on one lesson's problems? Open that lesson from the curriculum menu for the full re-teach.

explore.instructions: Identify each face of the rectangular time capsule box (l = 8 in, w = 5 in, h = 3 in). Find the area of each face pair, then calculate the total surface area.

discourse.prompt: The total surface area is 158 in². Which face pair contributes the most area? Why does that make sense when you look at the dimensions?
discourse.sentenceFrame: The ___ faces contribute the most area (___ in²) because their dimensions ___ × ___ = ___ are the largest. The total SA is ___ + ___ + ___ = ___ in².

diagram.instructions: Fold the flat net into the solid, then unfold it again. Every face you see in the net is a face you have to add up for surface area.

question.stem: This net has 6 rectangles. What does adding all 6 of their areas give you?
choices: The surface area of the solid

optional.stem: (Lesson 10.1) A time capsule box is 5 units long, 3 units wide, and 2 units tall. How many unit cubes fill it?
optional.explanation: V = length × width × height = 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cubic units.
choiceFeedback: Add the three dimensions, not multiply them. How many cubes fill the entire box?
Did you include all three dimensions? You need length × width × height.
Try multiplying the three dimensions in the order: length × width × height.
optional.stemEs: Una caja de cápsula del tiempo mide 5 unidades de largo, 3 unidades de ancho y 2 unidades de alto. ¿Cuántos cubos unitarios la llenan?
optional.explanationEs: V = largo × ancho × altura = 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 unidades cúbicas.
hints: Volume counts how many unit cubes fit inside a solid, so the answer will be in cubic units.
Use V = length × width × height and put all three given measurements into that formula.
Start with the bottom layer: 5 × 3 = 15 cubes in one layer. Now use the height to finish.
hintsEs: El volumen cuenta cuántos cubos unitarios caben dentro de un cuerpo, así que la respuesta irá en unidades cúbicas.
Usa V = largo × ancho × altura y coloca las tres medidas dadas en esa fórmula.
Comienza con la capa de abajo: 5 × 3 = 15 cubos en una capa. Ahora usa la altura para terminar.

optional.stem: (Lesson 10.2) A time-capsule box measures 6 in long, 4 in wide, and 3 in tall. What is its volume?
optional.explanation: V = length × width × height = 6 × 4 × 3 = 72 cubic in. Volume uses cubic units.
choiceFeedback: Are you adding the dimensions? Volume multiplies all edges: length × width × height.
You multiplied two dimensions but forgot the third — include length, width, AND height.
Check the units — this fills 3D space, so it needs cubic units, not square units.
optional.stemEs: Una caja para una cápsula del tiempo mide 6 in de largo, 4 in de ancho y 3 in de alto. ¿Cuál es su volumen?
optional.explanationEs: V = largo × ancho × alto = 6 × 4 × 3 = 72 pulgadas cúbicas. El volumen usa unidades cúbicas.
hints: Volume measures the space inside a solid, and it is always labeled in cubic units.
Use V = length × width × height: multiply two of the dimensions first, then multiply by the third.
Start with 6 × 4 = 24. Now multiply that result by the height of 3.
hintsEs: El volumen mide el espacio dentro de un cuerpo y siempre se escribe en unidades cúbicas.
Usa V = largo × ancho × alto: multiplica primero dos de las dimensiones y luego multiplica por la tercera.
Empieza con 6 × 4 = 24. Ahora multiplica ese resultado por la altura de 3.

optional.stem: (Lesson 10.3) You unfold a time capsule that is a cube. Its net shows 6 equal squares, and each square has an area of 4 cm². What is the cube's total surface area?
optional.explanation: A cube net has 6 equal square faces. With each face 4 cm², the surface area is 6 × 4 = 24 cm².
choiceFeedback: Multiply the face area by all six faces — don't just add the face count to the area.
A cube net has six faces, not four — multiply the face area by six.
Some faces are easy to forget in a net — make sure you count and include all six squares.
optional.stemEs: Desdoblas una cápsula del tiempo que tiene forma de cubo. Su desarrollo plano muestra 6 cuadrados iguales, y cada cuadrado tiene un área de 4 cm². ¿Cuál es el área total de la superficie del cubo?
optional.explanationEs: El desarrollo plano de un cubo tiene 6 caras cuadradas iguales. Con cada cara de 4 cm², el área de la superficie es 6 × 4 = 24 cm².
hints: A net shows every face of the solid laid out flat, so the surface area is simply the total of all the face areas.
The faces of a cube are all identical, so instead of adding six different numbers you can use repeated addition or multiplication.
Each square is 4 cm² and the net shows 6 of them, so set up 6 groups of 4 cm² and finish the multiplication.
hintsEs: Un desarrollo plano muestra todas las caras del sólido extendidas, así que el área de la superficie es simplemente la suma de las áreas de las caras.
Las caras de un cubo son todas idénticas, así que en lugar de sumar seis números distintos puedes usar suma repetida o multiplicación.
Cada cuadrado mide 4 cm² y el desarrollo muestra 6 de ellos, así que forma 6 grupos de 4 cm² y termina la multiplicación.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.1) What is the volume of a rectangular prism with l = 7 in, w = 3 in, h = 4 in?
approaching.explanation: V = l × w × h = 7 × 3 × 4 = 84 cubic inches.
choiceFeedback: Add 7 + 3 instead of multiplying? Volume uses multiplication of all three edges.
Square inches (in²) measure area, not volume. Volume is cubic (in³).
Multiply all three dimensions: 7 × 3 × 4, not 7 × 3 ÷ 2.
hints: Notice the three edge lengths: l = 7 in, w = 3 in, h = 4 in. Volume asks how much space fills the whole box.
Use the volume formula V = l × w × h, and remember volume is measured in cubic units (in³).
Start with 7 × 3 = 21 for the base, then multiply that result by the height, 4 inches.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el volumen de un prisma rectangular con l = 7 in, w = 3 in, h = 4 in?
approaching.explanationEs: V = l × w × h = 7 × 3 × 4 = 84 pulgadas cúbicas.
hintsEs: Fíjate en las tres aristas: l = 7 pulg, a = 3 pulg, h = 4 pulg. El volumen pregunta cuánto espacio llena toda la caja.
Usa la fórmula del volumen V = l × a × h, y recuerda que el volumen se mide en unidades cúbicas (pulg³).
Empieza con 7 × 3 = 21 para la base y luego multiplica ese resultado por la altura, 4 pulgadas.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.1) A time capsule box has a volume of 120 cm³. Its length is 10 cm and width is 4 cm. What is its height?
choiceFeedback: Check your division. 120 ÷ (10 × 4) = 120 ÷ 40 = ?
Did you use the formula h = V ÷ (l × w) correctly?
Verify: 10 × 4 × ? = 120. What number works?
hints: You already know the volume (120 cm³) and two edges (10 cm and 4 cm). The height is the missing piece.
Work backward: since V = l × w × h, divide the volume by the base area (length × width) to find the height.
First find the base area: 10 × 4 = 40 cm². Then figure out what number times 40 gives 120.
approaching.stemEs: Una caja de cápsula del tiempo tiene un volumen de 120 cm³. Su largo es 10 cm y su ancho es 4 cm. ¿Cuál es su altura?
hintsEs: Ya conoces el volumen (120 cm³) y dos aristas (10 cm y 4 cm). La altura es la pieza que falta.
Trabaja al revés: como V = l × a × h, divide el volumen entre el área de la base (largo × ancho) para hallar la altura.
Primero halla el área de la base: 10 × 4 = 40 cm². Luego averigua qué número por 40 da 120.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.2) What is the volume of a rectangular prism with l = 4 in, w = 3 in, h = 5 in?
approaching.explanation: V = l × w × h = 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 cubic inches.
choiceFeedback: Are you adding the dimensions? Volume multiplies all edges: length × width × height.
Check the units. Area is square units (²), volume is cubic units (³).
Not quite. V = l × w × h = 4 × 3 × 5 = ___ cubic inches.
hints: Spot the three edges: l = 4 in, w = 3 in, h = 5 in. Volume fills the whole box, so all three matter.
Use V = l × w × h and remember the answer needs cubic units (in³), not square units.
Multiply 4 × 3 = 12 for the base, then multiply that result by the height, 5 inches.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál es el volumen de un prisma rectangular con l = 4 in, w = 3 in, h = 5 in?
approaching.explanationEs: V = l × w × h = 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 pulgadas cúbicas.
hintsEs: Identifica las tres aristas: l = 4 pulg, a = 3 pulg, h = 5 pulg. El volumen llena toda la caja, así que las tres importan.
Usa V = l × a × h y recuerda que la respuesta necesita unidades cúbicas (pulg³), no cuadradas.
Multiplica 4 × 3 = 12 para la base y luego multiplica ese resultado por la altura, 5 pulgadas.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.2) A box has a volume of 36 cm³. Its length is 6 cm and width is 3 cm. What is the height?
choiceFeedback: That number is the length given in the problem — divide volume by the full base area to find height.
That's the width from the problem, not the height — divide the volume by length × width instead.
Check your division — find the full base area (length × width) before dividing into the volume.
hints: You're given the volume (36 cm³) plus two edges (6 cm and 3 cm). The height is what's missing.
Work backward: divide the volume by the base area (length × width) to uncover the height.
Find the base area first: 6 × 3 = 18 cm². Then ask what number times 18 gives 36.
approaching.stemEs: Una caja tiene un volumen de 36 cm³. Su longitud es 6 cm y su ancho es 3 cm. ¿Cuál es la altura?
hintsEs: Te dan el volumen (36 cm³) más dos aristas (6 cm y 3 cm). Lo que falta es la altura.
Trabaja al revés: divide el volumen entre el área de la base (largo × ancho) para descubrir la altura.
Halla primero el área de la base: 6 × 3 = 18 cm². Luego pregunta qué número por 18 da 36.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.3) A rectangular prism has l = 6 in, w = 4 in, h = 2 in. What is its surface area?
choiceFeedback: That's the volume — surface area needs the sum of all six face areas, not length × width × height.
Check the units — surface area covers a flat surface, so it needs square units, not cubic.
Remember each face has a matching opposite face — double the sum of the three face areas.
hints: Surface area covers all 6 faces of the 6 × 4 × 2 box — it's not the same as the space inside.
Use SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh: find the three different face areas, double each, and add.
Start with the top face: 6 × 4 = 24 in². Then find 6 × 2 and 4 × 2 before doubling and adding.
approaching.stemEs: Un prisma rectangular tiene l = 6 in, w = 4 in, h = 2 in. ¿Cuál es el área de su superficie?
hintsEs: El área superficial cubre las 6 caras de la caja de 6 × 4 × 2: no es lo mismo que el espacio de adentro.
Usa AS = 2la + 2lh + 2ah: halla las tres áreas de cara distintas, duplica cada una y suma.
Empieza con la cara de arriba: 6 × 4 = 24 pulg². Luego halla 6 × 2 y 4 × 2 antes de duplicar y sumar.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 10.3) How many faces does a rectangular prism have?
approaching.explanation: A rectangular prism has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back, left, and right.
choiceFeedback: Don't forget the top and bottom — a box has faces all around it, not just the sides.
That's the number of corners (vertices), not the number of flat faces.
That's the number of edges, not the number of flat faces — count the flat surfaces instead.
hints: Picture a cereal box in your hands. Turn it: there's a front, a back, two sides, a top, and a bottom.
Count faces in opposite pairs — every face on a rectangular prism has a matching partner across from it.
Count the pairs: top/bottom is one pair, front/back is another, left/right is the third. Multiply pairs by 2.
approaching.explanationEs: Un prisma rectangular tiene 6 caras: arriba, abajo, adelante, atrás, izquierda y derecha.
hintsEs: Imagina una caja de cereal en tus manos. Gírala: hay un frente, una parte trasera, dos lados, una tapa y una base.
Cuenta las caras en pares opuestos — cada cara de un prisma rectangular tiene una pareja igual del otro lado.
Cuenta los pares: arriba/abajo es un par, frente/atrás es otro, izquierda/derecha es el tercero. Multiplica los pares por 2.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 10.1) Two storage bins: Bin A is 8 × 6 × 5 inches. Bin B is 9 × 4 × 7 inches. Which holds more and by how much?
onLevel.explanation: Bin A: 8 × 6 × 5 = 240 in³. Bin B: 9 × 4 × 7 = 252 in³. Bin B holds 12 in³ more.
choiceFeedback: Calculate both volumes first: Bin A = 8 × 6 × 5 and Bin B = 9 × 4 × 7.
Which bin has the larger volume? Find the difference.
Check your arithmetic: 8 × 6 × 5 = ? and 9 × 4 × 7 = ?
hints: This is a two-part question: which bin holds more AND by how many cubic inches. You need both volumes first.
Find each volume with V = l × w × h, then subtract the smaller total from the larger to get the difference.
Start with Bin A: 8 × 6 = 48, then × 5. Next do Bin B: 9 × 4 = 36, then × 7. Compare the totals.
onLevel.stemEs: Dos cajas de almacenamiento: la Caja A mide 8 × 6 × 5 pulgadas. La Caja B mide 9 × 4 × 7 pulgadas. ¿Cuál guarda más y por cuánto?
onLevel.explanationEs: Caja A: 8 × 6 × 5 = 240 in³. Caja B: 9 × 4 × 7 = 252 in³. La Caja B guarda 12 in³ más.
hintsEs: Esta pregunta tiene dos partes: cuál caja guarda más Y por cuántas pulgadas cúbicas. Necesitas ambos volúmenes primero.
Halla cada volumen con V = l × a × h y luego resta el total menor del mayor para obtener la diferencia.
Empieza con la Caja A: 8 × 6 = 48 y luego × 5. Después la Caja B: 9 × 4 = 36 y luego × 7. Compara los totales.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 10.1) Added the Last Edge

workedExample.label: Dimensions
workedExample.work: A capsule is 6 long, 5 wide, and 3 tall

onLevel.correctWork: The student multiplied the first two edges correctly (6 × 5 = 30) but then added the height instead of multiplying it. Every edge must be multiplied: V = 6 × 5 × 3 = 90 cubic units.
hints: Look at the Calculate step. Was the height added or multiplied?
Multiply all three edges: 6 × 5 × 3 = 90 cubic units, not 6 × 5 + 3 = 33.
onLevel.explanation: The Calculate step starts fine with 6 × 5 = 30, but then the student writes + 3 instead of × 3, landing on 33. Volume multiplies every edge, so the correct work is V = 6 × 5 × 3 = 90 cubic units.
onLevel.explanationEs: El paso Calcular empieza bien con 6 × 5 = 30, pero luego el estudiante escribe + 3 en lugar de × 3 y llega a 33. El volumen multiplica todas las aristas, así que el trabajo correcto es V = 6 × 5 × 3 = 90 unidades cúbicas.
hintsEs: Mira el paso de calcular. ¿La altura se sumó o se multiplicó?
Multiplica las tres aristas: 6 × 5 × 3 = 90 unidades cúbicas, no 6 × 5 + 3 = 33.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 10.2) Two boxes: Box A is 10 × 5 × 4 inches. Box B is 8 × 6 × 5 inches. Which has more volume and by how much?
onLevel.explanation: Box A: 10 × 5 × 4 = 200 in³. Box B: 8 × 6 × 5 = 240 in³. Box B is bigger by 40 in³.
choiceFeedback: Recheck which box's volume is larger — recalculate both totals before comparing.
You picked the right box, but recheck the subtraction to find the exact difference.
These two volumes aren't equal — calculate each box's volume and compare the totals.
hints: This asks two things: which box holds more AND by how many cubic inches — so find both volumes first.
Compute each volume with V = l × w × h, then subtract the smaller total from the larger.
Box A: 10 × 5 = 50, then × 4. Box B: 8 × 6 = 48, then × 5. Compare the two totals.
onLevel.stemEs: Dos cajas: la caja A mide 10 × 5 × 4 pulgadas. La caja B mide 8 × 6 × 5 pulgadas. ¿Cuál tiene más volumen y por cuánto?
onLevel.explanationEs: Caja A: 10 × 5 × 4 = 200 in³. Caja B: 8 × 6 × 5 = 240 in³. La caja B es mayor por 40 in³.
hintsEs: Esto pregunta dos cosas: cuál caja guarda más Y por cuántas pulgadas cúbicas, así que halla primero ambos volúmenes.
Calcula cada volumen con V = l × a × h y luego resta el total menor del mayor.
Caja A: 10 × 5 = 50 y luego × 4. Caja B: 8 × 6 = 48 y luego × 5. Compara los dos totales.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 10.2) Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Dimensions
workedExample.work: A box is 6 in long, 4 in wide, and 1/2 in tall.

workedExample.label: Calculate
workedExample.work: V = 6 × 4 × 1/2, and the student dropped the 1/2: V = 6 × 4 = 24 cubic in

onLevel.correctWork: The student ignored the fractional edge of 1/2 in. A fractional edge still counts: V = 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 24 × 1/2 = 12 cubic in.
hints: Check Step 3: did the student use the 1/2 in height in the multiplication?
A fractional edge does not change the rule. Multiply all three: 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 12 cubic in, not 24.
onLevel.explanation: The Calculate step threw away the 1/2 in height, but a fractional edge is still an edge. Multiply all three: V = 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 24 × 1/2 = 12 cubic in. A half-inch height makes the volume half of 24, not equal to it.
onLevel.explanationEs: En el paso de calcular se descartó la altura de 1/2 in, pero un lado fraccionario sigue siendo un lado. Multiplica los tres: V = 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 24 × 1/2 = 12 pulgadas cúbicas. Una altura de media pulgada hace que el volumen sea la mitad de 24, no igual a 24.
hintsEs: Revisa el Paso 3: ¿el estudiante usó la altura de 1/2 en la multiplicación?
Una arista fraccionaria no cambia la regla. Multiplica las tres: 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 12 pulgadas cúbicas, no 24.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 10.3) A cube has edges of 5 cm. What is its surface area?
onLevel.explanation: A cube has 6 identical faces. Each face: 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Total SA = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².
choiceFeedback: That's the volume calculation (edge cubed) — surface area needs six face areas added together.
Check the units — a flat surface is measured in square units, not cubic.
Square the edge length for one face's area first, then multiply by the number of faces.
hints: A cube's 6 faces are identical squares, each one 5 cm by 5 cm.
Find the area of one square face, then multiply by 6 — and keep square units (cm²).
One face is 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Now multiply that area by the number of faces, 6.
onLevel.stemEs: Un cubo tiene aristas de 5 cm. ¿Cuál es el área de su superficie?
onLevel.explanationEs: Un cubo tiene 6 caras idénticas. Cada cara: 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Área total de la superficie = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².
hintsEs: Las 6 caras de un cubo son cuadrados idénticos, cada uno de 5 cm por 5 cm.
Halla el área de una cara cuadrada y luego multiplica por 6, conservando las unidades cuadradas (cm²).
Una cara es 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Ahora multiplica esa área por el número de caras, 6.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 10.3) Spot the Mistake — One Pair Was Not Doubled

workedExample.label: Read
workedExample.work: A time capsule box from the net is l = 7 in, w = 5 in, h = 4 in. Find the surface area.

onLevel.correctWork: The student doubled the first two pairs but forgot to double the left/right pair. There are two 20 in² faces, so it should be 2(20) = 40, not 20. Correct: SA = 70 + 56 + 40 = 166 in².
hints: Every face pair has 2 matching faces — check that each area is multiplied by 2.
The left and right faces are both 5×4 = 20, so add 40 in², not 20 in².
onLevel.titleEs: Detecta el error: un par de caras no se duplicó
onLevel.explanation: The three face areas are right, but the formula line doubles only the first two pairs. The left and right faces are each 5 × 4 = 20 in², so that pair contributes 2(20) = 40 in², not 20 in². The correct total is SA = 70 + 56 + 40 = 166 in².
onLevel.explanationEs: Las tres áreas de las caras están bien, pero la línea de la fórmula duplica solo los dos primeros pares. Las caras izquierda y derecha miden cada una 5 × 4 = 20 in², así que ese par aporta 2(20) = 40 in², no 20 in². El total correcto es SA = 70 + 56 + 40 = 166 in².
hintsEs: Cada par de caras tiene 2 caras iguales — revisa que cada área esté multiplicada por 2.
Las caras izquierda y derecha son ambas 5×4 = 20, así que suma 40 pulg², no 20 pulg².

extending.title: (Lesson 10.1) Find the Volume Error

workedExample.label: Dimensions
workedExample.work: l = 9 ft, w = 4 ft, h = 6 ft

extending.correctWork: 4 × 6 = 24, not 10. The student added instead of multiplied. Correct: V = 9 × 24 = 216 ft³.
hints: Check Step 3: what is 4 × 6?
4 × 6 = 24, not 10. The student added 4 + 6 instead of multiplying.
extending.explanation: Inside the Calculate step the student replaced 4 × 6 with 10, which is 4 + 6. Multiplying gives 4 × 6 = 24, so the volume is V = 9 × 24 = 216 ft³, not 90 ft³.
extending.explanationEs: Dentro del paso Calcular, el estudiante cambió 4 × 6 por 10, que en realidad es 4 + 6. Al multiplicar se obtiene 4 × 6 = 24, así que el volumen es V = 9 × 24 = 216 ft³, no 90 ft³.
hintsEs: Revisa el Paso 3: ¿cuánto es 4 × 6?
4 × 6 = 24, no 10. El estudiante sumó 4 + 6 en vez de multiplicar.

extending.title: (Lesson 10.2) Find the Volume Error
hints: Check Step 3: what is 3 × 2.5?
3 × 2.5 = 7.5, not 5.5. The student may have added instead of multiplied.
extending.explanation: In the Calculate step, 3 × 2.5 was written as 5.5, which is what you get by adding 3 + 2.5 instead of multiplying. Three groups of 2.5 make 7.5, so V = 5 × 7.5 = 37.5 m³.
extending.explanationEs: En el paso de calcular, 3 × 2.5 se escribió como 5.5, que es lo que se obtiene al sumar 3 + 2.5 en lugar de multiplicar. Tres grupos de 2.5 dan 7.5, así que V = 5 × 7.5 = 37.5 m³.
hintsEs: Revisa el Paso 3: ¿cuánto es 3 × 2.5?
3 × 2.5 = 7.5, no 5.5. Puede que el estudiante haya sumado en vez de multiplicar.

extending.title: (Lesson 10.3) Find the Surface Area Error

workedExample.label: Dimensions
workedExample.work: l = 10 in, w = 4 in, h = 3 in

extending.correctWork: The student forgot to multiply the last face pair by 2. It should be 2(4×3) = 24, not 12. Correct: SA = 80 + 60 + 24 = 164 in².
hints: Check Step 3: how many times does each face pair appear?
Each face pair has 2 matching faces. The student only counted one left/right face.
extending.titleEs: Encuentra el error del área de superficie
extending.explanation: The formula SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh is written correctly, but in the calculation the last face pair loses its 2. The left and right faces are each 4 × 3 = 12 in², so they contribute 2(12) = 24 in². The correct total is SA = 80 + 60 + 24 = 164 in².
extending.explanationEs: La fórmula SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh está escrita correctamente, pero en el cálculo el último par de caras pierde su 2. Las caras izquierda y derecha miden cada una 4 × 3 = 12 in², así que aportan 2(12) = 24 in². El total correcto es SA = 80 + 60 + 24 = 164 in².
hintsEs: Revisa el Paso 3: ¿cuántas veces aparece cada par de caras?
Cada par de caras tiene 2 caras iguales. El estudiante contó solo una cara izquierda/derecha.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Surface Area Using Nets is finding the area of only one face from each of the 3 matching pairs and forgetting to double it, instead of counting all 6 faces. For a box that is 9 in × 4 in × 5 in, a student might add just one face from each pair: (9×4) + (9×5) + (4×5) = 36 + 45 + 20 = 101 in², but the net actually has two of each face, so the correct total is 2(36) + 2(45) + 2(20) = 72 + 90 + 40 = 202 in² — exactly double. Before you submit, ask: 'Did I count both matching faces in each pair, or only one from each pair?'

diagram.title: Gift Box Face Pairs (in²)
diagram.caption: Each bar is one doubled face pair of the 14×10×6 box; add all three (280+168+120) to get the 568 in² of paper needed.

connect.scenario: A gift shop wraps boxes with decorative paper. A box is 14 inches long, 10 inches wide, and 6 inches tall. One sheet of wrapping paper covers 400 square inches.
connect.promptQuestion: How many sheets of wrapping paper are needed to cover the entire box?
connect.prompt: The box's surface area is ___ in² because SA = 2(___×___) + 2(___×___) + 2(___×___) = ___ + ___ + ___ = ___. You need ___ sheets because ___ ÷ 400 ≈ ___.

check.stem: What is the surface area of the box?
Why is each face pair multiplied by 2?
choices: A rectangular box has two identical faces of each size
Because you always double in geometry
Because there are 2 sheets of paper
check.explanation: Opposite faces of a rectangular prism match, so each of the three different face sizes appears twice.

check.stem: How many sheets of wrapping paper do you need?
check.explanation: 568 ÷ 400 = 1.42. One sheet is not enough, and you cannot buy 0.42 of a sheet, so you need 2 sheets.

connect.modelAnswer: SA = 2(14 × 10) + 2(14 × 6) + 2(10 × 6) = 280 + 168 + 120 = 568 in². Since 568 ÷ 400 = 1.42, one sheet is not enough — you need 2 sheets.

Check the units. Area is square units (²), volume is cubic units (³).
Are you adding the dimensions? Volume multiplies all edges: length × width × height.
hints: Note the edges: l = 7 ft, w = 2 ft, h = 3 ft — and remember volume answers use cubic units (ft³).
Apply V = l × w × h, multiplying all three edges, and pick an answer with cubic units.
Multiply 7 × 2 = 14 first, then multiply that result by the height, 3 feet.

questions.stem: How is volume different from area?
choices: Volume uses square units; area uses cubic units
Volume measures 3D space (cubic units); area measures 2D surface (square units)
Volume only applies to cubes; area applies to all shapes
questions.explanation: Volume measures the space inside a 3D shape (cubic units like in³). Area measures a flat 2D surface (square units like in²).
